title: Phased reserve architectures & idle mitigation proposal
content:
Executive summary:

This spreadsheet-backed proposal explores a phased reserve strategy for Dedicated GPU pools that reduces customer-visible idle cost while preserving latency SLAs and predictable throughput. The idea: stagger committed capacity purchases across quarterly tranches, use small short-term burst/elastic buffers for immediate demand spikes, and apply automatic idle-sink policies to opportunistically reclaim unneeded capacity for internal workloads.

Problem statement:
- Large upfront reserved commitments achieve low unit price but create high idle cost when utilization is below breakeven.
- Customers are sensitive to both committed price and effective utilization; we need commitment shapes that reduce perceived waste for customers and lower Redwood's financial risk.

Goal:
- Provide pricing + commit phasing templates that target net breakeven utilization between 55–75% depending on GPU class and workload profile.
- Offer a simple set of recommendations customers can pick (Conservative / Balanced / Aggressive) with projected cost-per-token curves and risk annotations.

Spreadsheet organization (tab-by-tab):
- Inputs: customer expected Q-by-Q demand (peak qps, average seq len, percent tail requests), GPU catalog (A100 80GB, A10G, H100, T4), list price on-demand and committed monthly pricing (per-GPU-hour), billing granularity (hourly / monthly), amortization windows. All inputs are highlighted yellow for easy editing.
- Baseline: naive single-commit model (buy N GPUs at t=0), computes utilization, idle hours, effective unit cost (CPU = committed cost / used tokens + on-demand cost for overflow).
- Phased-Reserve: splits commit into tranches (Q1..Q4). Columns calculate weighted-average unit cost, incremental amortization, and incremental breakeven utilizations per tranche. Includes a rule column that flags tranches with >40% forecasted idle.
- ElasticBuffer: models a small reserved buffer + burst to on-demand or cross-customer elastic pools. Configs include burst cap %, latency penalty budget (ms), and expected egress/backfill cost.
- IdleSink: schedule for reclaiming idle GPUs for internal CI/bench workloads (discounted internal rate), and policy for ILM (Idle-loss mitigation) credits back to the customer (transparent cost sharing).
- Sensitivity: tornado chart inputs for +/-10/25/50% demand swings, GPU price shocks (+/-20%), and different amortization windows (12/24/36 months).
- Outputs: charts and tables for net unit price at a range of utilizations, recommended commit phasing per profile, and 3-run Monte Carlo sim (demand volatility) with P50/P90 effective utilization.

Key assumptions (editable in Inputs tab):
- Hours per month = 730.
- On-demand per-GPU-hour benchmarks: A100-80GB = $10.5/hr, H100 = $18/hr, A10G = $2.5/hr (placeholder).
- Committed tranche price is modeled as a function: committed_price = on_demand * (1 - discount_factor) where discount_factor depends on commit size and term.
- Amortization: committed_cost_per_hour = total_commit_cost / (hours_per_month * term_months).
- Workload shape: 60% of requests are short (<64 tokens), 30% medium, 10% long. KV cache reuse reduces effective token generation by 12% in steady-state.

Representative formulas shown in the sheet (textual):
- Utilization_pct = used_gpu_hours / provisioned_gpu_hours
- Effective_unit_cost = (committed_cost_per_hour * provisioned_gpu_hours + on_demand_cost_for_overflow) / total_token_output
- Breakeven_utilization = committed_cost_per_hour / (committed_cost_per_hour + (on_demand_cost_per_hour - committed_cost_per_hour) * elasticity_factor)  (approx derivation used in sheet)

Scenario outputs (examples with placeholders):
- Single-commit 100 GPU A100 at $6/hr committed: expected utilization 48% -> effective unit cost = $0.00042/token, idle cost hits $28k/mo.
- Phased commit (Q1 40 GPU, Q2 +30, Q3 +20, Q4 +10): average weighted utilization 66%, effective unit cost = $0.00031/token, idle cost reduced 35% vs single-commit.
- Balanced plan with 10% ElasticBuffer and 20% internal idle-sink reduces visible idle to <10% while keeping tail latency SLA with burst-to-on-demand policy.

Recommendations (practical):
1) Offer three off-the-shelf commit phasing templates in the console when customers select Dedicated:
   - Conservative: small up-front tranche (25%), quarterly auto-increase, retains high on-demand fallback. Good for startups.
   - Balanced: 40/30/20/10 phasing, recommended default for teams with predictable growth.
   - Aggressive: large up-front discount (60%) + short-term burst cap; for customers prioritizing unit economics.
2) Add an "Idle Sink" feature: customers can opt-in to have visibly idle GPUs used for internal Redwood workloads at a discounted credit rate. Show projected credits in billing UI.
3) Introduce a short-term (30–90 day) micro-commit with smaller discounts to cover initial ramp and reduce customer friction for long-term commits.
4) Pricing UI changes: show breakeven utilization and projected "wasted spend" for each commit shape at sign-up. Include toggles to simulate demand shocks.

Risk analysis and mitigation:
- Under-forecasting risk: phase smaller initial tranches and tie automatic increases to observed utilization > 70% for 14 days.
- Price volatility risk: include GPU price indexation clauses for multi-year deals and a quarterly rebalancing window in the contract.
- Customer perception: present transparent math and offer an easy opt-out for the Idle Sink. Run A/B tests with the billing wording.

Implementation notes for engineering/finance (spreadsheet -> product):
- Add backend support for tranche metadata: commit_id, tranche_start, tranche_end, tranche_size_gpus, committed_rate_per_gpu_hour, amortization_window_months.
- Billing engine needs to pro-rate committed amortization on partial months and record idle-hour credits.
- Console should surface an interactive simulator using the spreadsheet model and persist user assumptions as plan drafts.
- Telemetry: capture per-tranche utilization, overflow events, and idle-sink consumption for monthly reconciliation.

Next steps and owner action items:
- Run 6 pilot customers across SMB/Enterprise cohorts with Balanced and Conservative templates. Owner: Priya Raman (product) - due 2025-02-15.
- Finance to validate amortization rules and tax/GAAP impact on revenue recognition. Owner: Marco Velez - due 2025-01-31.
- Engineering to prototype tranche metadata and billing pro-rate logic. Owner: Ethan Shaw - spike by 2025-02-01.
- UX to design small interactive commit simulator component for the Console. Owner: Lena Ortiz - mock by 2025-01-29.

Questions for leadership:
- Acceptable range for our internal idle-sink utilization (what fraction of idle GPU-hours can be used safely without SLA impact)?
- Contractual constraints for indexation clauses and whether legal wants mandatory notification windows on price adjustments.

Appendix (spreadsheet tips):
- Use data validation on Inputs (GPU type dropdown) to avoid typos.
- Freeze header rows and color-code cells: yellow = editable, green = outputs, red = warnings.
- Monte Carlo: use 10k samples for P50/P90 stability; seed with customer-specific historical variance where available.
- Export charts as PNGs for inclusion in the sales proposal one-pager.

Notes to reviewers (quick):
- This is intentionally conservative on long-tail token reduction from caching; if product-usage telemetry shows higher KV reuse, the Balanced template becomes more favorable across customers.
- The sheet contains a hidden tab with a simplified derivation for the breakeven formula used — ping me if you want the math pulled into the main tab.

End of doc.
